newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Euro-MPs urge EU action to police cyber-space.
newsitem.headline: Euro-MPs urge EU action to police cyber-space.

text.p: The European Parliament on Thursday called for European and international action to drive illegal pornographic, paedophile and racist material off the information superhighway, the Internet.

Parliament acknowledged it was extraordinarily difficult to police the global computer network, which is now used by over 50 million people worldwide, but said the authorities, industry and users all had to take what action they could.

European Union governments should set up teams of cybersleuths to trawl the Net for evidence of crime, especially child sex rings, sects and neo-Nazi literature, and give their police more powers to pursue Internet abusers at home and in other member states, Euro-MPs said in a report.

They urged Internet service providers to adopt a code of conduct which would oblige them to report to the police any illegal or offensive material sent through their system -- using websites, newsgroups or electronic mail -- and then wipe it out.

Parliament recognised there was very little to stop criminals from bypassing obstacles and sending new messages, using a different access provider or shifting base to another country where the same material is not considered illegal.

It was essential therefore for EU countries to introduce common rules in their criminal law and press for an international accord defining clearly what constituted illegal content, so that those involved could be prosecuted wherever the provider was based, the parliament said.
Europe also needed common rules determining who was liable for material on the Net, including making service providers criminally responsible if they made illicit material available.
This worries some service providers, who argue that telephone companies are not prosecuted when criminals contact each other by phone.
One of the most promising methods for cleaning up cyberspace, in Euro-MPs' eyes, is specialised software which filters out filth.
This allows online service providers or parents to block access to offensive material. One example is a system which, when triggered, simply disconnects the user.
EU Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann told Euro-MPs on Wednesday the European Commission was actively working on drafting Internet regulation.
But he warned that even European-level efforts would be insufficient and that international action was essential.
The parliament's recommendations come only days after Germany indicted a local head of online service CompuServe for allegedly aiding in the dissemination of pornography on the Net.

The German parliament last week began debating tough draft laws to fight illegal misuse of the global computer -- the first Western country to do so -- and is being watched closely by the Commission in Brussels.
German police investigations against CompuServe began in 1995 and the company then took the unprecedented step of banning access to millions of its members worldwide to over 200 newsgroups.

The move caused an outcry among CompuServe users and cyber-rights groups in the United States, who were outraged that German authorities could exercise such influence over what Americans were able to read and view online.
The European Parliament acknowledged there was a delicate balance between protecting the public from cyber-criminals and respecting their right to freedom of speech and privacy.
Censorship of Internet providers -- such as that practiced by countries like China and Singapore -- ran counter to fundamental democratic principles, Euro-MPs said.
